newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FOCUS-S.Korea refiners face dilemna over pollution.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Korea refiners face dilemna over pollution.

text.p: South Korean refiners face a dilemna over how to match up to tougher pollution laws that will be implemented in coming years, industry sources said on Tuesday.
The new laws will demand lower levels of harmful sulphur in oil products for the domestic market.
The refiners, who process 2.44 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude, could invest in new refinery units to take out the sulphur, or buy more crude oil that is low in sulphur to start with.
But both options will be expensive, analysts said.
Low sulphur crude is more expensive that higher sulphur crude and more limited. Asian buyers are increasingly importing from as far away as West Africa because regional crude sources are drying up.
Building desulphurising units would be a better solution, analysts said, but refiners are hesitant to pay for such costly projects at a financially difficult time.
"South Korean refiners face a severe shortage of desulphurising facilities," said Moon Young-seok, an analyst at Korea Energy Economic Institute.
"They have no choice but to bring in more low-sulphur crude or products," he said.

South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said the sulphur content in fuel oil would be reduced to 0.5 percent from 1.0 percent from July 1997 in urban areas and from 1999 for the rest of the country.

The sulphur content in diesel for cars would be lowered to a maximum of 0.05 percent in April 1998, from the current 0.1 percent, to match levels in industrialised countries such as the United States or Japan.

A maximum of 0.1 percent sulphur content in diesel, which is used as an industrial fuel as well as for home heating, will be enforced throughout the country in July 1997. It is currently fixed at a maximum of 0.1 percent for urban areas only.

The ministry also said it will gradually reduce the sulphur content in kerosene, which is used mostly for heating, although it has no set targets. The sulphur content is currently set at a maximum of 0.08 percent, which is relatively high considering Japan's 0.008 percent, analysts said.

South Korea's refining sector has expanded rapidly in recent years, but analysts and industry officials said refiners failed to build up enough desulphurising capability to meet future environmental standards.
South Korea currently has a middle distillate desulphurising capacity of 549,000 barrels per day (bpd) and a heavy oil desulphurising capability of 65,000 bpd, the ministry said.
The sector has plans to raise the middle distillate desulpherisation capacity by 110,000 bpd to 659,000 bpd by next year and fuel oil by 90,000 bpd to 155,000 bpd by early 2000.
But demand is already outstripping those levels.
Government data show demand for middle distillates is expected to be 719,500 bpd and fuel oil 442,000 bpd in 1997.
"It would take time for refiners to set up new desulphurisers because they are so expensive," said an official at the ministry.
The new units would cost each refiner in the range of $70-$140 million, industry sources said.
"Refiners can't afford to build additional desulphurisers because of their poor financial status," Moon said.
Profits of South Korean refiners were savaged last year, largely as a result of foreign exchange losses. Major refiners are also burdened with debt as a result of huge facility expansion.
Last year, Hyundai Oil Refinery Co and Yukong Ltd added 200,000 bpd refining capacity each and LG-Caltex Oil Corp 220,000 bpd.
Analyst said some refiners doubted whether it would be economical to build such costly desulphurisers.
"Some refiners think it would be cost-effective to import low-sulphur crude or products than to set up a new desulphuriser," said Moon.
